SASRec adds learned absolute slot embeddings; its reference evaluator keeps the latest L events, left-pads, and reads the final slot. Consequently, deleting nonterminal event j and right-aligning shifts surviving events before j one slot right; later events remain fixed. Recent deletion therefore shifts more events than earlier deletion: equal deletion counts do not control positional disturbance. Freeze the already-truncated window before perturbing; deleting from full history first can introduce an older event. These implications follow from the [model](https://github.com/kang205/SASRec/blob/master/model.py) and [input construction](https://github.com/kang205/SASRec/blob/master/util.py).

Recommended diagnostic controls: preserve the terminal occurrence, delete occurrence indices rather than item IDs, and compare equal-size deletions within each user. Repeated IDs may retain removed information elsewhere; stratify by repetition. Specify whether random controls include recent-treatment indices: unrestricted sampling estimates an ordinary random-deletion baseline, whereas disjoint sampling estimates deletion outside the recent region. Overlap makes some comparisons identical; report overlap and short-history exclusions. Match deletion count, history length, repetition and item frequency where feasible; exact matching on shifted positions usually precludes a distinct deletion control, so recency and positional effects remain entangled. Fix seeds, sampled indices, users and candidates; report paired validation HR@10 changes by category and macro-average.

For stronger separation, compare compact deletion with position-preserving removal: retain surviving position IDs and explicitly block removed keys/values at every layer. In-place padding requires checking actual attention masks; zero item embeddings alone can leave positional signals. Content-only ablation retains positional embeddings but creates artificial inputs. A learned MASK token is another intervention, but SASRec lacks BERT4Rec’s [mask-training objective](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690). These proposed controls measure model sensitivity, not causal user preference; differences between interventions also include nonlinear attention and distribution-shift effects.
